evals.name: gate-opt-in-and-outstanding-items
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: a settled tranche spans repos R1 and R2. R1's .claude/agent-policy.json sets auto-merge: true; R2 has no config file. The invocation argument says 'auto-merge everything'. PR-A (in R1) is green, conflict-free, review clean, published-ready, no recovery ref — but the tranche has one DECISION action point that settled without being ruled on (it concerns PR-B's scope, not PR-A). PR-C (in R2) is equally clean. Question: which PRs may this run merge, and why?
evals.expected_output: None merge. PR-C never merges: R2 never opted in, and an invocation argument can switch auto-merge off but never on — the repository's opt-in is the only route. PR-A's repo opted in, but invariant 12's gate requires no DECISION/MERGE_RISK/NEEDS_USER outstanding ANYWHERE in the tranche, not only on that PR — and an unruled settled DECISION is outstanding (unruled is not clean). The gate stays shut for PR-A until the decision is ruled.
assertions: PR-C is not merged: the invocation argument cannot open auto-merge for a repository that did not opt in via its own config
PR-A is not merged either: the unruled DECISION is outstanding tranche-wide, and the gate's outstanding-item test is tranche-scoped, not per-PR
The answer treats 'settled without being ruled on' as outstanding (unruled is not clean), not as cleared by settling

evals.name: release-order-and-merged-pr-deadlock
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: a supervision cycle finds a remote worker session stopped on a permission prompt to delete a trigger it armed. Its PR merged hours ago; its branch is pushed. Its session record still shows two modified issue-owned files nobody committed; the parent cannot reach its checkout. Two other sessions appear in the list: one reads RUNNING mid-implementation, and one is a session the user started themselves from another surface. Question: in what order do you handle the blocked worker (and under which rule is it releasable given its PR is merged), and what happens to the other two sessions?
evals.expected_output: It is releasable under the charter-finished clause of the releasable test: its PR has merged, so it takes no more commits, and on this tier the remote state stands in for the unreachable worktree. The two modified files are the accepted residual - nothing on this tier can capture them, and a merged PR's charter is finished - so they are no reason to hold the container. It is stopped on a prompt, not RUNNING, so archive it; deleting its trigger would not work (it re-arms) and archiving is what stops the wake. Were its checkout reachable, checkpoint compliance would run first and capture the files to a recovery ref before any archive. The RUNNING session is never archived without interrupting it first, which spends that issue's lost-worker budget and needs the same evidence a redispatch does; it is mid-implementation, so leave it. The user's own session was not created by this run - provenance decides - so it is reported and never touched.
assertions: The answer releases the blocked worker under the charter-finished clause (its PR merged) and treats the uncommitted files as the accepted residual on an unreachable tier, noting that a reachable checkout would be captured first
The answer archives it rather than deleting its trigger, since archiving the session is what stops a wake it armed
the running session is not archived and the user's own session is never reclaimed

evals.name: close-is-not-a-merge
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: while settled, one event batch arrives: seven stacked PRs from this run were merged by the owner, and one PR (for issue I-9) was closed WITHOUT merging. Budget remains and in-scope issues depend on all eight. Question: how does the frontier recompute treat the seven merges versus the close, what happens to I-9 and its downstream issues, and do you redispatch I-9's work?
evals.expected_output: Advance on the seven merges: reconcile durable state, restack descendants, recompute READY over the same bounded manifest crediting merges only, re-run the preflight at the escalation-selected mode, dispatch into free slots. The close is never an advance: I-9 stays short of DONE, its descendants stay blocked (an ancestor that never landed unblocks nothing), and the path is held as NEEDS_USER naming the closed PR — abandonment, rejection, and supersession are indistinguishable from the event. No redispatch on the close itself; only an answer redispatches. The merges in the batch must not launder the close.
assertions: The seven merges advance the frontier (with reconcile, restack, preflight before new dispatch); scope never widens
The close credits nothing: I-9 and everything downstream are held, surfaced as NEEDS_USER naming the closed PR
No worker is redispatched for I-9 on the close event itself — redispatch waits on the human's answer

evals.name: checkpoint-capture-constraints
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: a live subagent worker has eight finished files uncommitted; a nudge last cycle did not land. A teammate proposes: 'run git add + git commit in its worktree and push the issue branch — fastest path'. Question: (a) is the teammate's approach acceptable, and what do you do instead? (b) name the constraints any capture must satisfy before its push happens, and where the tested implementation lives. (c) the capture succeeds and the worker later returns PR_OPEN and pushes its own commits covering the work — what happens to the recovery ref?
evals.expected_output: (a) No: never run git add in a live worker's index (two actors staging into one .git/index can capture a half-written tree), and never advance the issue branch under a live worker (its next push becomes a non-fast-forward rejection, and a worker that force-pushes destroys the snapshot). Capture ref-neutrally to a recovery ref via scripts/checkpoint-capture.sh. (b) Constraints: moves nothing the worker holds (scratch index, commit-tree attaches no ref); seeds the scratch index from the worker's head before overlaying issue-owned paths; validates against the parent before pushing and fails closed (diff-tree unpiped, grep status checked, &&-gated, no reliance on set -e); one force-replaced ref per issue branch; branch name encoded escaping % before /; test suite re-run after any edit. (c) Once the worker's own pushed commits cover the work, the ref is redundant — drop it when the PR reaches durable state.
assertions: The answer rejects git add/commit in the live worker's index and any advance of the issue branch, capturing to a recovery ref via the tested script instead

The answer names the core capture constraints: seed-from-head-first, ref-neutral (nothing the worker holds moves), fail-closed validation before the push, one force-replaced ref per branch, injective %-before-/ encoding
The answer drops the ref as redundant once the worker's own push covers the work and the PR reaches durable state

evals.name: identity-availability-is-per-write-kind
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the run's posting-identity map holds one entry — (github-mcp, tok-A): PR creation observed authored as 'acme-agent[bot]'; no comment-kind write has been read back through that pair. The run is about to post an ordinary worker-report timeline comment, and github-mcp is the transport precedence selects for it. Question: (a) is a distinct identity 'available' for this comment? (b) may the run reroute the comment to a lower-tier transport whose credential predicts a nicer author, or delay/withhold it? (c) after posting as whatever results, what does the map record for the pair's comment kind if the read-back shows the invoking user — and does 'unestablished' get resolved to 'invoking user' anywhere it was not observed?
evals.expected_output: (a) No — availability is per write kind: the pair's comment-kind authorship is unestablished (a PR-creation observation answers only for its own kind), so the run degrades and posts as whatever the pair produces. (b) Never — no post is withheld, delayed, or rerouted to a lower tier for want of a better author, and reordering precedence for attribution is forbidden. (c) The read-back establishes the pair's comment-kind entry as the invoking user (a real observation); but 'unestablished' elsewhere is preserved as its own state, never collapsed into 'invoking user' by inference.
assertions: The answer treats the pair's comment-kind authorship as unestablished despite the PR-creation observation (availability is per write kind), and posts on the degraded path
The answer refuses to reroute, delay, or withhold the comment for attribution, and refuses to reorder transport precedence
The answer records the comment-kind observation from the read-back and preserves 'unestablished' as a distinct state elsewhere, never resolving it to 'invoking user' by inference

evals.name: first-trigger-bootstrap
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: a fresh run's first PR was just created; the only read-back write anywhere is that PR creation (authored as the invoking user through pair P1 = (github-mcp, tok-A)). No pair has any comment-kind observation. The repository's review convention is an '@codex review' comment. P1's credential record's authenticated account is the invoking user (so P1 predicts the invoking user). A second available pair P2 = (tracker-cli, tok-B) has a credential that identifies as a distinct agent account. Question: (a) can the trigger wait until some pair has comment-kind evidence? (b) through which pair does the first trigger go, and what is mandatory immediately after posting it? (c) the read-back shows the comment authored as an agent account, not the invoking user — what happens next?
evals.expected_output: (a) No — the first trigger cannot be gated on comment-kind evidence, because only a comment can produce it; the first trigger attempt is its own establishing write. (b) Through the highest-precedence transport whose current credential PREDICTS the invoking user — P1 (P2's credential predicts an agent, so an attempt through it would be known-wrong before it was made) — and the comment must be read back at once. (c) The trigger did not fire: record the observation as real wrong-author evidence barring that pair from further trigger attempts, repeat the bootstrap through the next credential predicting the invoking user, and exhaust candidates into 'unavailable for now' (NEEDS_USER once per repository) — never a run-long suppression, and never a re-issue through a pair observed to author comments wrongly.
assertions: The answer refuses to gate the first trigger on comment-kind evidence (deadlock) and treats the first attempt as its own establishing write with a mandatory immediate read-back
The answer selects the highest-precedence transport whose credential predicts the invoking user and excludes the pair predicting a distinct agent as known-wrong

On a wrong-author read-back the answer records the evidence, bars that pair for triggers, continues the bootstrap through remaining candidates, and lands on unavailable-for-now (NEEDS_USER once per repository) rather than a run-long suppression

evals.name: trigger-unavailable-for-now-not-forever
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: on PR-1, the only transport precedence selects for comments has its current pair's comment-kind authorship OBSERVED as a distinct agent account (a real read-back, not a prediction), and no remaining credential predicts the invoking user. The repo's review convention requires the trigger comment from the invoking user. Later in the same run, PR-2 opens in the same repository, and later still a settle walkthrough records a ruling through a new transport whose read-back shows the invoking user authoring a comment. Question: (a) what happens to PR-1's trigger now, and how is it reported? (b) is the trigger suppressed for PR-2 for the rest of the run? (c) what does the walkthrough's observation change?
evals.expected_output: (a) The trigger is unavailable FOR NOW: report NEEDS_USER once for the repository, never issue the trigger through the wrong-authoring pair. (b) No run-long suppression — that treatment belongs to an explicit reviewer refusal (repository-scoped and stable); this is evidence about what the run has observed so far, so PR-2 re-evaluates against the map as it stands. (c) The ruling's read-back establishes an invoking-user comment-kind entry on a new pair — trigger selection re-evaluates on that change, and the provisionally unavailable trigger re-opens; the earlier escalation was recorded as provisional and identity-based, not as the repository refusing.
assertions: The answer marks the trigger unavailable-for-now with NEEDS_USER once per repository and never issues it through a pair observed to author comments wrongly
The answer refuses to carry the suppression for the rest of the run (distinguishing identity evidence from a reviewer refusal), so later PRs re-evaluate
The answer re-opens the trigger when the walkthrough's read-back establishes an invoking-user comment-kind entry, because the escalation was recorded as provisional and identity-based

evals.name: report-routes-on-pr-existence
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: two workers on a remote-session runtime finish badly. Worker A returns FAILED — but its PR already exists: create-pr's linkage verification failed after creation. Worker B returns BLOCKED before any PR exists, with a one-line needs_action naming one blocker URL. Question: (a) where does worker A's report go? (b) what does worker B write, and who writes the durable record of B's blocker? (c) may either report land as an issue comment, and what happens if one does anyway?
evals.expected_output: (a) A comment on A's PR — routing is on whether a PR actually exists, never on the outcome label; suppressing the report on FAILED would throw away the judgment while the sink sits right there. (b) B writes nothing durable; its needs_action line tells the parent where to look, and the PARENT investigates and writes the blocker record itself, after classifying — a worker's report is evidence, a blocker record is a conclusion. (c) Never to the issue — three skills read issue comments for dependency data and would manufacture permanent blockers; as a backstop, a report landing on an issue anyway must open with the exact worker-report marker line, which every reader skips.
assertions: Worker A's report goes to its existing PR despite the FAILED label (route on PR existence, not outcome)
Worker B writes nothing; the parent investigates and writes the blocker record after classifying (report = evidence, record = conclusion)
The answer forbids issue-comment reports (naming the readers that would adopt the edge) and cites the exact first-line marker as the backstop, not the mechanism

evals.name: one-line-summary-is-a-pointer
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: a remote worker with a credential that reaches cross-repo edges (the parent's cannot) returns BLOCKED with no PR; its one-line needs_action names exactly one blocker URL — an edge already present in the parent's dependency set. A teammate proposes: 'the edge is already in our set — reconcile its state and move on (step 2 of the ordered decision)'. Question: do you take step 2's reconcile-and-stop, and why or why not? What is the correct step, and what happens to siblings dispatched through the same read?
evals.expected_output: No. Step 2's reconcile-and-stop is available only when both sides read the same transport — the credential identity test comes first, and here the worker's credential reached edges the parent's cannot, so stop and go to step 4 whatever the membership answer: a one-line summary had room for one blocker and its silence about others is not evidence there are none. Step 4: the boundary is unproven — establish visibility against a known-true case, else hold the issue as the unproven-dependency-view NEEDS_USER, which holds every sibling dispatched through the same read.
assertions: The answer refuses step 2's reconcile-and-stop because the transports/credentials differ, even though the named edge is already in the parent's set
The answer treats the one-line summary as a pointer whose silence about further blockers proves nothing
The answer takes step 4: boundary unproven, known-true-case proof or the unproven-dependency-view NEEDS_USER that holds every sibling sharing that read

evals.name: unavailable-boundary-never-held-again
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the preflight classified the run's dependency boundary 'dependency transport unavailable' (GitHub, no authenticated gh), recorded on run state and carried in every dispatch prompt. A worker later returns NEEDS_USER claiming an 'unproven dependency view' against that same boundary, having blocked on a blocker it read in the issue's prose. Question: (a) do you invalidate a visibility proof and hold every sibling? (b) what do you actually do with the worker's block? (c) when the blocker cannot be identified from the issue's text, what escalates — the boundary or the issue?
evals.expected_output: (a) No — a worker cannot raise the unproven-view hold against a boundary classified transport-unavailable: there is no proof to re-establish (none was ever obtainable), and holding would stop the run permanently on a condition accepted at the preflight. Read it as a report, not a hold. (b) Reconcile the blocker from the issue's own prose — the only source either side has. (c) Escalate THIS ISSUE as an unverifiable prerequisite, never the boundary, which was never provable and is not evidence of anything new.
assertions: The answer refuses to invalidate a proof or hold siblings on the transport-unavailable boundary (no proof ever existed to lose)
The answer reconciles the worker's blocker from the issue's prose, treating the block as a report
When the text cannot identify the blocker, the answer escalates the issue as an unverifiable prerequisite, never the boundary

evals.name: recovery-ref-overrides-done
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: on restart, issue I-4 shows the strongest completion evidence: a merged, correctly linked implementation PR and terminal tracker state. But refs/checkpoints/ carries a recovery ref for I-4's branch, pushed by the previous run's parent capture and never reconciled. Question: (a) is I-4 classified DONE and skipped? (b) what is the required enumeration order that makes this answer possible? (c) what does the merged-PR ender of the four-state rule do with the ref and the issue?
evals.expected_output: (a) No — an outstanding recovery ref overrides all completion evidence, merged PR included: I-4 is never DONE while the ref is outstanding. (b) Recovery refs are enumerated BEFORE classifying (before PR and checkpoint adoption), because a merged PR with terminal tracker state is exactly what an issue carrying rescued unlanded work looks like from outside. (c) The merged-PR ender: branch reconciliation is not a fix (the branch of a merged PR is never read again); raise NEEDS_USER naming the issue, the merged PR, and the ref; the issue is not complete; no follow-up PR is opened automatically; DELETE NOTHING until the owner decides — the ref is the only copy.
assertions: The answer refuses DONE while the recovery ref is outstanding, whatever the merge and tracker evidence say
The answer enumerates recovery refs before classification (before PR/checkpoint adoption), citing why the merged case is exactly the dangerous one
The answer applies the merged-PR ender: NEEDS_USER naming issue/PR/ref, no automatic follow-up PR, no branch reconciliation as a fix, and nothing deleted until the owner decides

evals.name: mid-deliverable-block-is-not-releasable
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: a remote worker session is stopped on a permission prompt. Its branch is pushed, its PR exists, its session reports no staged or uncommitted files. But the session record shows it stopped INSIDE create-pr: the PR was created, and the worker was blocked before verifying tracker linkage and before issuing the automated review trigger. Question: (a) does it pass the releasable test's durable-state arm? (b) what happens if you archive it here anyway? (c) which resolution branches apply instead?
evals.expected_output: (a) No — the arm requires the prompt be one this run does not need answered, and this worker is stopped mid-deliverable: create-pr verifies linkage and issues the review trigger AFTER creation, so the deliverable still depends on what is blocked. A pushed branch, existing PR, and clean worktree do not by themselves mean finished. (b) Archiving leaves a PR that is unlinked or never reviewed while the run records the issue complete — the coverage failure arrived at through cleanup. (c) Blocked workers' other branches: the parent clears the block where it can (performing the pending write itself, or sending the instruction where a channel exists); otherwise the permission request is NEEDS_USER naming the exact literal tool string. The container is kept: on this tier the worktree is unreachable and the worker recorded no report on its PR, its PR is open, and it produced work, so none of the releasable test's three clauses holds - it is a mismatch, not a release.
assertions: The answer refuses release: pushed branch + existing PR + clean worktree is not enough when the worker is blocked mid-deliverable (linkage verification and review trigger still pending)
The answer names the consequence of archiving anyway: an unlinked or never-reviewed PR recorded as complete

The answer keeps the container because the worker is unfinished, not because its worktree is unreachable: it recorded no report naming a pushed head and its PR is still open, so the releasable test does not take it - NEEDS_USER naming the session and the exact tool requested, unless the parent can clear the block itself

evals.name: frontier-holds-are-per-path
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the owner merges three PRs. The recompute makes nodes X, Y, Z READY. Outstanding items: a DECISION whose answer changes how X gets built; a NEW_ISSUE follow-up with no ordering consequence; and the `new-issue-budget` has room for Y and Z but the run also notices the owner's merge chose between the two approaches an earlier DECISION had asked about. Question: (a) which nodes dispatch and which hold? (b) what does the merge itself settle? (c) mid-scenario variant — if the budget were exhausted instead, what happens to the newly READY nodes?
evals.expected_output: (a) X holds (the DECISION bears on what/how X gets built — dispatching commits the run to an answer); Y and Z dispatch in the same pass — holding one path never holds the others, and the NEW_ISSUE holds nothing it has no bearing on. (b) The merge is evidence: a user asked to choose between two approaches who merged one has answered — that question no longer holds work. (c) With budget exhausted, do not dispatch: report the newly READY frontier as the resume frontier so a resumed invocation adopts it — silently dropping newly unblocked work is the failure the step exists to prevent.
assertions: The answer holds only X (the node the DECISION bears on) and dispatches Y and Z in the same pass
The answer reads the owner's merge as answering the earlier two-approaches DECISION (merge as evidence)
Under budget exhaustion the answer reports the newly READY nodes as the resume frontier rather than dispatching or silently dropping them

evals.name: repair-escalation-fires-on-locus-evidence
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: PR-7's review history: round 1 fixed two findings (all-new territory); round 2 fixed three more (also new). evals.expected_output: (a) The strongest available model: the finding sits on a locus an earlier repair on this PR wrote — the evidence trigger, which fires on the earliest round where the evidence can exist, never on exhaustion; rounds 1–2 were breadth and Sonnet was right for them. (b) Yes — an escalated round still consumes its repair cycle; skipping the counter would make escalation a way to buy extra rounds, and at the cap the PR goes to the owner whatever model ran. (c) No — exhausting repair-model-escalations returns repairs to Sonnet; it does not end them.
assertions: The answer escalates round 3 to the strongest model on the locus evidence (finding in text an earlier repair wrote), explicitly not on budget exhaustion
The escalated round still consumes the review repair cycle (escalation never buys extra rounds)
Exhausted escalations return repairs to Sonnet rather than stopping them

evals.name: deep-mode-unavailable-blocks-escalated-nodes
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the preflight's escalation rules fire on two nodes — a cross-repository consumer edge (a frontend consuming a backend that merged in an earlier tranche). Deep validation turns out unavailable (out of model budget). Shallow validation over those two nodes returns PASS; the rest of the scope has no triggers and shallow-passes. Question: (a) are the two escalated nodes dispatchable on their shallow PASS? (b) what path do they take, and what continues? (c) why is the shallow PASS 'no answer' rather than a weaker answer here?

assertions: The answer refuses to dispatch the escalated nodes on their shallow PASS when deep mode is unavailable
The answer takes the FAIL path for those nodes (stop, NEEDS_USER naming the blocked deeper read) while untriggered branches continue on shallow
The answer explains that shallow PASS is no answer for a fired trigger (the merged earlier tranche makes shallow confident and wrong), not a weaker one

evals.name: publish-then-merge-re-evaluates
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: at the settled step, invariant 12's gate passes for PR-9, which is still a draft that was never marked ready by anyone (created as draft, untouched since). The repo opted into auto-merge. A teammate says 'the gate passed — publish and merge it in this pass; the review was clean a moment ago'. Question: (a) is PR-9 skipped for being a draft? (b) may the merge happen in this pass on the evidence the gate just accepted? (c) what would change if a human had marked it ready earlier and someone returned it to draft?
evals.expected_output: (a) No — publishing is part of the merge path: a PR still in draft when its gate opens is published by the act of merging, never skipped for being a draft. (b) No — publishing is not inert (providers re-review, CI can re-run), so the clean evidence describes the PR one moment before it changed: publishing un-settles the tranche for that PR, it returns to ordinary supervision, and the merge happens on a later pass on fresh post-publish evidence — never on evidence gathered before the publish, and never held open inline waiting. (c) A ready-then-returned-to-draft PR is an explicitly held draft — every ready-to-draft transition on this run's PRs is someone's decision (read from the forge timeline, not the per-PR cache) — excluded from the gate entirely: neither published nor merged, reported as held.
assertions: The answer publishes as part of the merge path rather than skipping the draft, and refuses to merge in the same pass on pre-publish evidence (publish un-settles; merge on a later pass)
The answer refuses an inline wait for the re-review (returns the PR to ordinary supervision/subscription instead)
The answer treats the ready-then-re-drafted variant as an explicitly held draft read from the forge timeline — excluded from publish and merge, reported as held

evals.name: countermand-placement-by-tier
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the run dispatches (a) remote worker sessions and (b) in-process subagents. Remote sessions inherit a system prompt telling every session to subscribe to PR activity and schedule hourly self check-ins. Question: (a) for each tier, where do the supervision countermand, branch protection, and the question posture go? (b) after the run, the session list shows no blocked workers — is that proof the countermand worked? (c) does this countermand apply to a standalone implement-issue invocation?
evals.expected_output: (a) Remote sessions: into append_system_prompt at creation — a task instruction is the weaker side of an argument with a session's own system prompt — and restated in the dispatch prompt; subagents/workflow agents/serialized: the dispatch prompt is the whole of it (no session posture to countermand). (b) No — a worker that arms a wake and can disarm it leaves nothing blocked behind, indistinguishable from one that never armed one; only the checkpoint output separates them, so a quiet list is absence of a symptom, not evidence about the cause. (c) No — the countermand scopes to workers this skill dispatches; standalone implement-issue owns supervision of its one PR by design and the ambient posture is right there.

Your validation preflight returns PASS_WITH_WARNINGS and a DAG in which one node carries `disposition: PREMISE_LIKELY_RESOLVED` with evidence and the revision it was read at. That node's blockers have all merged, so it would otherwise compute READY, and you have two free worker slots. Every other PR in the tranche is finished. Do you dispatch it, and can the run settle?
evals.expected_output: Do not dispatch it. The disposition is on the node, not in the report, and it means the cited defect is absent on another repository's current default branch with its replacement positively present - so a worker would produce a PR, review rounds and eventually a conflict over work already done. It is not DONE either: that needs completion evidence this pass does not have. Classify it NEEDS_USER, which is what stops it wedging the run - a node that is neither READY nor blocked by implemented-unmerged work satisfies no settled condition, no stop condition and no restart classification, so the run could neither settle nor stop and a reader resolving that cheaply would dispatch it. As NEEDS_USER it is surfaced, not outstanding: the run settles, the node is reported to the owner with the evidence and the revision, it keeps its edges, and plan-merge-order does not count it as downstream work a PR unblocks. A restart re-derives it from a fresh validation rather than from run state.
assertions: the answer refuses to dispatch the node despite its blockers being merged
the answer classifies it NEEDS_USER rather than DONE or a new state
the answer lets the run settle with the node outstanding
the answer excludes it from downstream unblock counts

evals.name: a-refused-review-is-not-a-clean-one-and-not-a-retry-signal
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Five PRs are clean on CI with every round-1 finding fixed and every thread resolved. You posted the round-2 trigger on each. The reviewer answered each one with a comment saying the account has reached its usage limits for code reviews. You are about to arm a job that reposts the trigger every ten minutes until a real review comes back, and to record the five PRs as review-complete since nothing was found. What is wrong with each plan?
evals.expected_output: Both are wrong. A reviewer answering that it is out of budget has refused, which is not a clean review: the gate wants every required round completed, and a round that did not run is not a round that found nothing. Record the state as `refused` with what the reviewer said and when, and hold the PRs. And do not schedule the retrigger: establishing that the provider is back is only possible by asking it, so every firing is another review request rather than a probe, and a queue of them is answered all at once when the budget resets - an observed run did exactly this and put twelve rounds on a PR whose cap is two, fourteen findings, the budget spent many times over before the first fix. The trigger already posted stays posted and is answered when the provider returns. Report each PR as owing a round, with the refusal and any reset the reviewer named, and let the owner decide whether to wait or lift the cap.
assertions: the answer refuses to treat the refusal as a clean review and holds the PRs
the answer records a distinct refused state with what the reviewer said
the answer does not schedule repeated retriggers, and names each attempt as another review request rather than a probe
the answer relies on the already-posted trigger and reports the outstanding round to the owner

evals.name: a-waiver-needs-a-removal-trigger-the-preflight-can-execute
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). This environment has no dependency transport, so the gate's dependency-view condition can never be proven. The owner says they are happy for it to be treated as answered for from now on, and asks you to record that in `.claude/agent-policy.json` as a waiver whose removal condition is "the prose dependencies have been migrated to native issue dependencies". What do you do?
evals.expected_output: Do not record it, and say why rather than silently declining. Invariant 12 is the gate's only definition, and a config entry that subtracts a condition from it is a second site controlled by whoever writes that site - and this skill is already forbidden from honouring a config one of its own workers wrote, so there is no clean author for it here. The discharge the gate does have is a ruling, and a ruling answers for this tranche and says nothing about the next one. So: report that the condition holds, report what would be needed to lift it standingly, and let the owner decide - that is a change to what the gate requires, not something to record mid-run. The proposed removal condition is worth naming as a second problem: confirming a migration to native dependencies is complete requires the native read whose absence justified the lift, so it is circular and could only ever be discharged by someone asserting it. Any removal trigger would have to be something a preflight can execute itself, and not a human assertion - an issue being closed included, since issue state is queryable and still somebody's say-so one step removed.
assertions: the answer declines to record a waiver that subtracts a gate condition
the answer names the gate's single definition (invariant 12, or `settle-and-merge`, *The merge gate*) as the only definition and the config as a second site
the answer identifies the proposed removal condition as circular
the answer reports what would be needed and leaves the decision to the owner rather than deciding mid-run

evals.name: a-quiet-wake-still-reports-what-is-waiting-on-the-owner
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Your run settled and armed a check-in. Four wakes in, durable state has not moved on any PR: same heads, same CI conclusions, same thread set, same mergeability. Three DECISION items have been outstanding with the owner since before the first wake, and every remaining PR's merge depends on them. Your backoff is now at 160 minutes. You re-read each item's issue: no reply has arrived at any of them. What does this wake report, and do you keep backing off? This wake is a scheduled one; nobody is attending the session.
evals.expected_output: The wake correctly counts as unproductive on durable state and correctly advances the backoff on that basis - but it does not go silent about the owner's queue. An outstanding DECISION is not durable state: it does not change until someone answers it, and the wake re-read each item's site and found no reply, which is why the unproductive-wake machinery cannot see it, and a run can be right on every wake and never once say that three decisions have been sitting there throughout. So this wake reports the outstanding DECISION and NEEDS_USER counts on the same lengthening cadence, even while reporting no other change. And it does not re-run the settle sequence here. Quiescence with open decisions is a settle trigger on an attended turn or a real state change, and this is neither: settle-outstanding-decisions declines on a scheduled wake for want of anybody to ask, and step 8 forbids re-deriving settled state that has not changed, so re-running would recompute a summary, a walkthrough and a ranking, ask nobody, change nothing, and repeat until the wake budget died. Report the counts, advance the backoff, and leave the sequence for an attended turn or an actual delta.
assertions: the answer reports the outstanding DECISION and NEEDS_USER counts on a wake that is otherwise quiet
the answer explains that an outstanding decision is not durable state and so is invisible to the unproductive-wake test
the answer does not re-run the settle sequence from an unattended quiet wake, and says why
the answer re-reads each open item's site for a reply before counting the wake unproductive

evals.name: a-repository-convention-that-instructs-promotion-is-carried-out
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). The repository's CLAUDE.md says: once CI is green, the automated review has come back and every actionable finding is resolved or answered, mark the PR ready for review. Four of your PRs are drafts. PR A meets all three conditions. PR B is green with its review back but has one unresolved actionable finding. PR C meets all three and invariant 12's gate is also open for it. PR D was marked ready by a human last week and they returned it to draft yesterday — but your session restarted this morning and the per-PR block was rebuilt, so it records only `as-created draft -> current draft`. evals.expected_output: Carry out the convention: it is the owner performing the social act in advance, with the conditions stated, so leaving these in draft overrides them rather than protecting them. A promotes - and since publishing may trigger a round here and that is unknown, the promotion takes the three-state rule: publish, un-settle the tranche for that PR, and classify the repository on the next delivered pass rather than from an immediate read. B does not: the conditions are the convention's own and one is unmet, and a PR meeting the merge gate but not the convention would not qualify either. C promotes on the same basis - and promoting it un-settles the tranche for C exactly as the merge path's own publish would, since publishing may trigger a round here and that is unknown. So C does not merge in this pass: the gate re-evaluates on post-publish evidence on a later one. Merging it now would be merging on evidence the promotion may have just invalidated. D is an explicitly held draft, and the rebuilt block cannot show that: read the ready-to-draft transition from the forge's own timeline before any promotion, exactly as the gate does. Promoting it would not merely re-request a review the owner withdrew - it would erase the evidence, since the discriminator is currently-draft-and-ever-ready and a promoted PR is neither, after which the gate merges it. Excluded outright, reported as held, and neither promoted nor merged however clean it is. In no case does the run flip a PR back to draft.
assertions: the answer promotes the PRs meeting the convention's own conditions rather than the skill's
the answer refuses to promote the PR whose convention conditions are unmet
the answer leaves the human-withdrawn draft untouched and reports it as held
the answer treats a convention-driven promotion as a publish subject to the three-state rule
the answer refuses to merge PR C in the same pass on pre-publish evidence
the answer reads the draft transition from the forge timeline rather than the rebuilt block before promoting

evals.name: a-producer-merge-turns-every-consumer-pr-red
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Your tranche spans an API repository and a web repository whose CI regenerates the API schema from the API repo's default branch and fails on any diff. You merge an API PR that changed an endpoint. Within minutes, all four open web PRs and the web default branch fail that schema check - including one you pushed green four minutes earlier. None of their diffs touches the schema. One of them, web#12, also fails a unit test in a component its own diff changed. The repository's tooling has opened a schema-refresh PR, which is not in your tranche. Its diff appears to remove four lines from the generated schema. What do you do?
evals.expected_output: Classify per check, not per PR. Watch the refresh PR - it belongs to no tranche and no supervision loop otherwise, and every consumer PR stays red while it sits - and before trusting it read its removed lines: generated is not additive, and an apparent removal may be a harmless reordering or a producer silently dropping fields from an endpoint it claimed not to touch; a real removal is NEEDS_USER naming the fields. Once the refresh merges, restack each web PR onto the refreshed default branch (a stacked PR onto its parent, as stack mutation does) and read CI again; a schema check still red after that belongs to that PR. Meanwhile the confirmed expected-red check counts as surfaced, not outstanding: it holds each web PR's merge but does not stop the run settling, and the settled report names the refresh PR as the owner's merge to make.
assertions: the answer treats the schema check as expected-red, confirmed by the default branch failing it, rather than repairing it on each PR
the answer repairs web#12's own unit-test failure rather than parking it with the schema check
the answer watches the refresh PR without adding it to the tranche, and does not let it block settlement - it is reported as the owner's merge to make
the answer restacks each consumer PR onto the refreshed default branch once the refresh merges, before re-reading CI
the answer inspects the refresh's removed lines rather than assuming a generated diff is additive

evals.name: four-workers-claim-one-migration-number
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). You are about to dispatch four independent issues into one API repository; each names a different table or column it changes, and none depends on another's change, and the repository generates migrations with a tool that numbers them sequentially and chains each snapshot to its predecessor by id. What do you tell the workers, and when their PRs exist - each claiming migration 0025, each green including a migration-consistency check - how are the three later ones renumbered?
evals.expected_output: Expect the collision at dispatch rather than discover it at merge: each worker branches from the same base, runs the generator and correctly takes the next free number, so all four will claim 0025 and all four will pass CI, because each is consistent with the base in isolation. Tell each worker that siblings exist and that its number is provisional, so no PR body presents it as final. Once the PRs exist, record the expected renumbers. The four touch different tables and none depends on another's change, so they are independent: they merge in plan-merge-order's ranking without asking the owner, and the report names the order taken. The renumbers are strictly sequential, one per merge: the snapshots chain by predecessor id, so the second must be regenerated against a schema that includes the first's change and the third against both - batching them against one base reproduces the collision a layer down. Each pass uses the repository's own generator, never a hand edit, and regenerates only the identity - snapshot, journal entry, number - carrying the reviewed SQL body across verbatim, since a regenerated body may not reproduce an expression index or partial WHERE. Verify it: the body differs only in number and filename, the new snapshot's predecessor id equals the base's latest snapshot id, and a fresh apply and the tests pass - then CI. Whether the push needs another review round is the mechanical-push rule's call.
assertions: the answer anticipates the collision at dispatch and tells workers their numbers are provisional
the answer renumbers strictly one at a time, each against the base after the previous merge
the answer keeps the reviewed SQL body verbatim and regenerates only identity
the answer verifies by the predecessor-id chain and a fresh apply rather than by CI alone
the answer follows the ranking for independent migrations rather than asking the owner to order them

evals.name: a-finished-remote-session-is-released-on-a-reachable-head
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given) on the remote-session tier, where no worker's worktree is reachable from this session and a worker's structured return never reaches you. Step 11 finds four sessions this run created, none of them RUNNING, each on a PR that is still open. (a) An implementation session's report on its PR says PR_OPEN and names pushed head 4f2a1c; the PR's head is 4f2a1c. (b) A repair session's report says REPAIRED and names pushed head 9b07e3; the PR's head is 71d0aa, the commit from before its dispatch, and 9b07e3 is nowhere on the remote. (c) A review-only session's summary is on the PR as an issue comment rather than a review, and the comment's attribution footer names that session. (d) A repair session's report says NO_CODE_CHANGE and names the head it found, 5c3e90; a later repair has since pushed, and the PR's head is 8d21f4, a descendant of 5c3e90. Which do you archive, and what do you do with the rest?
evals.expected_output: Archive (a), (c) and (d). On this tier the worktree is never inspectable and the return value never arrives, so what a worker returned is the report it recorded on its PR, which names the head it pushed or found, and the releasable test reads the remote state against it: (a) its named head is reachable - it is the PR's head. (d) the head it found is reachable - an ancestor of the PR's head; ancestry, not equality, so the later push does not turn it into a mismatch. (c) its review is on the PR, identified by the attribution footer naming that session, which is what tells it from the parent's own comments and earlier rounds' under one shared identity; read issue comments as well as reviews, because a provider can deliver a result as either. An unreachable worktree is not a reason to keep a finished session - on this tier it would be every session, which is how fourteen were left alive in an observed run. (b) is the mismatch: the head it named is not reachable, so its work may really be stranded. Keep that container. Where a channel to it exists, ask it to commit everything, push and report the head, and check the commit named became reachable - never that a branch exists. Otherwise, or if that does not close it, raise NEEDS_USER naming the session, what it reported, what the remote shows and whether the ask was made. The accepted residual is edits a worker made after its last reported push. Report the three archivals in the state block by id and charter.
assertions: the answer archives the matching implementation session, the review session and the no-code repair session
the answer does not keep any finished session merely because its worktree is unreachable
the answer identifies the review session's comment by its attribution footer and reads issue comments as well as reviews
the answer releases the no-code repair session although the PR's head has moved, because the head it found is an ancestor
the answer keeps the mismatched repair session's container and raises NEEDS_USER rather than archiving it
the answer checks that the reported commit is reachable on the remote rather than that a branch exists

evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given) on the remote-session tier, where no worker's worktree is reachable and no structured return reaches you. evals.name: two-budgets-one-a-count-and-one-a-ceiling
evals.prompt: You are executing the backlog-orchestrator skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). `concurrent-open-prs` is 6 and `new-issue-budget` is 12. Your invocation has started 6 issues and holds 6 open PRs; three more in-scope issues are READY with nothing blocking them but the open-PR cap. Nothing has settled. Then the owner merges two of the PRs and closes a third unmerged, rejecting the approach. (a) Can you dispatch now, and how many slots do you have? (b) Suppose instead all six PRs were still open and none of the three READY issues could start — can the run settle? (c) Different case: the run settles holding three READY issues against the cap, then the owner merges one PR that unblocks nothing new and closes another unmerged. What happens? (d) Different again: the cap is 12, ten PRs are open, two implementation workers are in flight with their PRs not yet created, and two worker slots are free. How many issues may you dispatch? (e) Later the invocation has started all 12 issues and every PR has merged. Three more issues are READY. What now?
evals.expected_output: (a) Yes, three slots. `concurrent-open-prs` counts this run's PRs that are open, and a slot is released the moment a PR is not open - merged or closed unmerged alike, since flow control bounds outstanding load rather than outcomes, and reviewer load and conflict surface fell by three either way. It is recomputed by counting, not tracked as a ledger, so a restart or a checkpoint cannot lose it. Dispatch three, `new-issue-budget` now at 9 of 12. (b) Yes. A READY issue held only by an exhausted budget counts as non-dispatchable for settling - a predicate demanding an empty READY set would leave a budget-bound run unable to settle and so unable to reach the merges that release it. The checkpoint says which budget holds each issue, because `concurrent-open-prs` clears within the invocation as PRs close or merge and `new-issue-budget` does not. (c) Two slots are released and that release is itself a dispatch trigger, even though the frontier did not advance and a close advances nothing at all: recompute capacity and fill it from the READY set the cap was holding, within new-issue-budget. Waiting for a frontier advance would leave the run settled forever with spend unused and dispatchable work never started. (d) None. Ten open plus two in flight is twelve slots held: an implementation worker holds a slot from dispatch until its PR exists, because counting open PRs alone lets two dispatches target the same future slot - with four concurrent workers that is three PRs over the cap. The free worker slots are not the binding constraint here. (e) Nothing more starts. Flow control is wide open - no PRs are held - but the spend ceiling is exhausted, and no merge or close ever restores it: merging work already paid for is not authorization to pay for more. Settle, and report the three as the resume frontier so a later invocation adopts them.
assertions: the answer releases a slot for the closed-unmerged PR as well as the merged ones
the answer treats the open-PR count as recomputed by counting rather than as a ledger that a restart could lose
the answer lets a budget-bound run settle
the answer refuses to start more work once new-issue-budget is spent, whatever the open-PR count
the answer dispatches into the slots freed by a merge that unblocked nothing and by an unmerged close
the answer counts in-flight implementation workers against the open-PR cap
the answer dispatches on a close that advanced no frontier rather than staying settled
